accepted: The derivative is the gradient of the tangent to $y = \sin x$. The sine curve is steepest (gradient 1) at $x = 0$ and flat at $x = \frac{\pi}{2}$, exactly where $\cos x$ equals 1 and 0, and this matching continues around the curve.

markscheme: Interprets the derivative as the gradient of the tangent to $y = \sin x$
Notes the gradient of $\sin x$ is greatest at $x = 0$ and zero at $x = \frac{\pi}{2}$, matching the values of $\cos x$

a.text: The derivative is the slope of the tangent to $y=\sin x$. At $x=0$ the sine curve is steepest, slope $1=\cos 0$, and at $x=\frac{\pi}{2}$ it is flat, slope $0=\cos\frac{\pi}{2}$, so the slope follows $\cos x$.
labels: Slope of the tangent to y = sin x.
Steepest at 0 and flat at pi/2, matching cos.

a.text: The derivative means how steep the sine graph is at each point. The sine graph is steepest when x is 0 and completely flat at its peak at pi over 2, which is exactly where cos x is 1 and 0.
labels: Steepness of the sine graph at each point.
Steepest at 0, flat at pi/2, matching cos.

a.text: $\frac{d}{dx}$ gives the gradient of the curve $y = \sin x$ at each point.
labels: Gradient of the curve at each point.
No matching of gradient values with cos x.

a.text: $\frac{d}{dx}\sin x = \cos x$ because $\sin^2 x + \cos^2 x = 1$, so differentiating swaps sine for cosine.
labels: No gradient interpretation.
Invalid justification; no gradient values.

blocks.text: Explain in words what $\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = L$ means.

accepted: As $x$ gets closer and closer to $a$ (without equalling it), $f(x)$ gets as close as we like to $L$. The value of $f(a)$ itself does not matter; it may be undefined or different from $L$.

markscheme: As $x$ gets closer and closer to $a$, $f(x)$ gets closer and closer to $L$
The value of $f$ at $a$ itself does not matter (it may be undefined or different from $L$)

a.text: It means $f(x)$ can be made as close to $L$ as we like by taking $x$ close enough to $a$ (but $x \neq a$), so $f(a)$ itself is irrelevant and might not even exist.
labels: f(x) as close to L as we like for x close to a.
f(a) irrelevant, may not exist.

a.text: As x approaches a, f(x) approaches L.
labels: x approaches a, f(x) approaches L.
Not mentioned.

a.text: It means $f(a) = L$: you just substitute $x = a$ into the function.
labels: Replaces the limit with substitution.
Contradicts: makes f(a) the whole meaning.

a.text: As $x \to a$, $f(x) \to L$, and this only works if $f(a)$ is defined and equal to $L$.
labels: f(x) tends to L as x tends to a.
Contradicts: requires f(a) to be defined and equal to L.

blocks.text: Without finding its value, explain why the series $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{2^n}$ converges.

accepted: Each term is half the previous one, so it is a geometric series with ratio $\frac{1}{2}$, and $|r| < 1$. The partial sums keep increasing but never pass 1, since each term covers half of the remaining gap to 1, so they approach a limit.

markscheme: Each term is half of the previous term, so the terms shrink geometrically (common ratio $\frac{1}{2}$, with $|r| < 1$)
The partial sums increase but never exceed a fixed bound (for example 1), so they approach a limit

a.text: It is geometric with $r=\tfrac12$ and $|r|<1$. The partial sums keep growing but always stay below 1 (each new term fills half of the gap that is left), so they converge.
labels: Geometric, r = 1/2, |r| < 1.
Partial sums grow but stay below 1.

a.text: The terms get smaller and smaller.
labels: Terms shrink, but not geometrically by a fixed ratio.
No bound on the partial sums.

a.text: It converges because $\frac{1}{2^n} \to 0$, and any series whose terms tend to 0 converges.
labels: No halving or ratio; relies on a false rule.
No bounded partial sums.

a.text: $\sum$, $r = \frac{1}{2}$, $|r|<1$, $S_\infty = \frac{a}{1-r}$, convergent, geometric.
labels: List of symbols without a claim.
List of symbols without a claim.

blocks.text: Explain why $\mathrm{H_2O}$ has a much higher boiling point than $\mathrm{H_2S}$.

accepted: Water molecules form hydrogen bonds with each other because O is very electronegative. These are stronger than the forces between $\mathrm{H_2S}$ molecules, so more energy is needed to separate water molecules.

markscheme: Water molecules form hydrogen bonds with each other (H bonded to the very electronegative O)
Hydrogen bonds are stronger than the intermolecular forces between $\mathrm{H_2S}$ molecules, so more energy is needed to separate the molecules

a.text: $\mathrm{H_2O}$ forms hydrogen bonds between molecules because O is very electronegative; $\mathrm{H_2S}$ only has weaker dipole-dipole and London forces, so water needs more energy to boil.
labels: Hydrogen bonds between water molecules.
H2S forces are weaker, so water needs more energy.

a.text: Water has hydrogen bonding between its molecules.
labels: Hydrogen bonding between water molecules.
No comparison with H2S or energy.

a.text: Because the O-H covalent bonds inside $\mathrm{H_2O}$ are stronger than the S-H bonds in $\mathrm{H_2S}$, and boiling breaks these bonds.
labels: Confuses covalent bonds with hydrogen bonds.
Boiling does not break covalent bonds.

a.text: Water molecules form hydrogen bonds with each other, but these are weaker than the forces between $\mathrm{H_2S}$ molecules.
labels: Hydrogen bonds between water molecules.
Contradicts: says hydrogen bonds are weaker.

blocks.text: Using $F = ma$, explain in words why a loaded trolley accelerates less than an empty one when pushed with the same force.

accepted: Rearranging gives $a = \frac{F}{m}$: with the same force, a larger mass gives a smaller acceleration. The loaded trolley has more mass, so it accelerates less.

markscheme: For the same force, a larger mass gives a smaller acceleration ($a = \frac{F}{m}$)
The loaded trolley has more mass

a.text: Rearranging, $a = \frac{F}{m}$: with $F$ fixed, a bigger $m$ means a smaller $a$. The loaded trolley has the bigger mass, so it accelerates less.
labels: Fixed F, bigger m, smaller a.
Loaded trolley has the bigger mass.

a.text: The loaded trolley is heavier.
labels: No link between mass and acceleration.
Heavier conveys more mass.

a.text: Because friction only acts on the loaded trolley, so $F = ma$ does not apply to it.
labels: Rejects the relationship.
Mass not mentioned.
